title: Half Past Five
segment_text:
## Chapter 1 — Half Past Five

The woman came up the back stairs at ten to five with a navy coat over her arm, and asked whether they could take it up an inch and a half.

Alison looked at the clock that had been on that wall since before she came, and said they could.

Nobody had told her, and that was the whole of it. And still she had come up the back stairs the way women had come up the back stairs since 1904, because the fourth floor did alterations and she wanted a coat taking up.

"You're not shutting, are you," the woman said, in the voice of somebody who had read something and decided it was about a different shop.

"We're open till half five," Alison said, which was true, and was the only true thing she could manage.

She put her on the box in front of the three-way mirror. The woman stood the way they all stood, chin up, arms out from her sides like a scarecrow apologising. Alison knelt. Her knees took a second to agree, the way they did now. She turned the hem under and pinned it and stood back and looked, and it was an inch and a half. You knelt down and you pinned it and you let her watch herself in the mirror while you did.

"That's better," the woman said. "Isn't that better."

"It'll hang now," said Alison.

The machine had a lot number on it — a small orange sticker under the balance wheel, LOT 114, put there by a young man from the auctioneers who had said *lovely old thing* about a Singer that had outrun three managers. Alison unpicked, pressed, turned it and ran the seam, and the machine did exactly what it was asked and nothing more.

Forty minutes. She pressed it twice, because a coat is worth two pressings, and put it on a hanger and brought it out.

"What do I owe you?"

"Nothing today."

"Don't be daft."

"Nothing today," Alison said. "Go on."

And the woman, who had a bus to catch, went, calling something over her shoulder about coming back at Christmas with a skirt.

At half past five the lights went off in the lift lobby, and somebody in the stockroom was crying and would not want it known. Alison put her scissors and her good tape measure in her bag, because they were hers, and left the rest.

On the wall by the door were the hooks, and on hers a strip of masking tape with HOYLE on it in biro, in her own hand, written in 2001. She got a thumbnail under the corner. It came away in one piece, which surprised her. She put it in her pocket.

Then she turned off the light over the bench.

The room did not go dark. It stayed exactly as it was — the tables, the mirror, the chalk dust in the boards — because it was a north window, and it had always been the window.
cliffhanger: There is a table standing empty in the Lantern that nobody has wanted for two years.

title: What She Was Worth
segment_text:
## Chapter 2 — What She Was Worth

The letter came with the second post, which meant she was in, because she was in now.

It thanked her for twenty-six years in a font chosen by somebody in an office she had never seen, and explained, in a paragraph she read three times, that the enhanced part was discretionary and had been exercised in her favour. At the bottom it said twenty-one thousand five hundred and seventy pounds.

She put the kettle on.

She had not meant to do the division. But the envelope was in her hand and there was a biro from a bookmaker's she had never been in, and by the time the kettle clicked off she had written 21,570 divided by 26 down the side of the envelope in her mother's handwriting, which is to say her own.

Eight hundred and twenty-nine and something. Call it eight hundred and thirty.

Eight hundred and thirty pounds for a year. For the year she took up eleven bridesmaids in a fortnight and finished the last one at ten past midnight. For the year Gary went, when she came in at half eight every morning and did the work and said nothing, and Pauline said nothing either, correctly.

Then she was annoyed with herself, which took about an hour and did not get her anywhere.

The phone went at four, when the sun got round to the front room, being a first-floor flat over what had been the Co-op.

"Well," said Sylvia. "What are you going to do now, then."

"I'm having a think."

"A think." Her mother left it exactly where she had put it. "You've never had a think in your life. You've a lad in Glasgow and a machine in the spare room and you're fifty-two."

"Fifty-two's not —"

"I know what fifty-two is. I've been it. Have you got money?"

"I've got money."

"Well, then," said Sylvia, in a tone that closed the subject and did not close it at all.

She brought the machine through after tea. It weighed more than a person expects and less than her back believed, and she set it on the kitchen table because there was nowhere else, and the bread board went on the side by the toaster where it did not belong.

She did not sew anything. She sat with the letter and a cup of tea going cold and did not sew anything.

At eleven she got up to go to bed and stopped in the doorway.

The Singer sat under the kitchen light with its wheel and its plate and its long black neck, plugged into nothing. She looked at it the way you look at a horse in a hallway. A good horse. An animal with no business where it was and no way of getting out.
cliffhanger: The table is under the worst of the draught and the best of the light.

title: The Lantern
segment_text:
## Chapter 3 — The Lantern

She went down on the Thursday to look, which is what she told herself on the way.

It had been the Market Hall on the deeds since 1877 and the Lantern in every mouth in the town since about 1950, on account of the eleven glazed lanterns down the spine of the roof, which let down a light no architect since has managed to buy. It smelt of pastry and cut keys and cardboard and cold stone. The columns had been touched up in four different greens by four different men, each of whom had been certain he had matched it.

The empty pitch was by the north door. Thirty-one pitches, twenty-two let, and this one standing empty since a fortnight before the first lockdown.

"Draught's shocking," said Hilary Ashworth, who had arrived beside her without any noise at all. "That door's a nuisance from November."

"It's the best light in the building."

Hilary looked at her.

"It is," she said.

The table was deal, scarred all over, with a bit of somebody's chewing gum under the near edge gone the colour and hardness of a shirt button. On the front board, under forty years of hands, was a ghost sign in signwriter's script: T. CRABTREE & SON · NOTHING OVER 50p.

"Seventy-two pound a week," Hilary said. "All in. That's your leccy, your bins, insurance for the building, not for your stock. There's a leak over pitch seven and everything's under there in a bucket."

"What's the notice?"

"Month either way." She had a ring of keys on her belt that hung to her knee. Alison counted them later, over months, without meaning to: thirty-one. "You'd be sat next to Kelly's coffee. She'll talk at you, but she's no trouble."

Alison did not remember agreeing. She remembered her mouth saying go on, then, which is what you say to a child offering you a sweet, and the whole of it taking less time than a hem.

She scrubbed the table on Friday morning with a bucket and a green pad and the water came off the colour of tea. She emptied it and did it again and it came off the colour of tea again. She stopped after that, on the grounds that a table has a right to some of its own history, and dried it with a towel from home, and the wood came up warm and pale and shocked, like a face out of a scarf.

Then there was nothing to do.

She stood behind it at four o'clock with her hands flat on it. Kelly's chalkboard said CAMOMILLE. Bernie Fazakerley was telling a customer something about her sister the customer had not asked to know. Above her the eleven lanterns let their light down the way they had done for a hundred and forty-nine years — over her, and her table, and her hands.

And every soul in that building was looking at her, kindly, and had already decided how long she would last.
cliffhanger: The first customer comes at nine minutes past ten, and she is not ready.

title: A Knee
segment_text:
## Chapter 4 — A Knee

The first customer came at nine minutes past ten and Alison was not ready, and thought afterwards that she never would have been.

She was young, twenty-six or so, in a coat too thin for the hall, holding a Co-op bag with both hands the way you hold a thing that has got heavier than what is in it. She stood at the corner of the table a moment, not quite arrived.

"Are you doing repairs?"

"I am."

"It's only —" She stopped, and started again, and Alison could hear the rehearsal in it, the sentence built in a kitchen and carried down Corn Street. "It's his school trousers. Both knees have gone. I bought them six weeks since, in July, for starting back, and he's been in them four days."

"Let's have a look."

Grey polyester, age eight, both knees out the way they go — not a tear, a scuff and then a hole, from a boy going down on tarmac at speed because he is eight and the world is worth it. There was a second pair in the bag with one knee gone.

"I've tried patches. Off the internet. They come off in the wash."

"They do."

"I've no more uniform money till —" and she stopped again and looked at the table, and Alison looked at the trousers, because there are moments when the kindest place in the world to put your eyes is on the work.

"I'll put a proper patch in behind and darn over the top," Alison said. "Nothing's invisible on a knee. But it'll go through to Christmas, and when he goes through it again, and he will, you bring them back and I'll do it again."

"How much?"

And there it was. She had thought about this for a week and a half and had a piece of paper at home with numbers on it, crossed out and written again, and not one of them arrived. What arrived was four.

"Four pound."

"For all three knees?"

"For all three knees."

The woman got her purse out and paid in coins, and one of them was a fifty, and Alison did not look at it and did not say anything about it.

She did the work while she waited, because Kelly had a chair going spare and it was nine minutes past ten. Twenty minutes a knee. She did them the way she would have done a lining on the fourth floor, and she hated herself for about an hour afterwards — four pound, four pound, a woman of my age — and then somewhere in the afternoon she stopped, and did not start again.

The young woman folded the bag over and said thank you twice and went.

At the north door she stopped. She looked back down the hall — past Kelly, past the coffee, at the table, and at Alison behind it — for about as long as it takes to read a sign.

Then she went out into Corn Street, and the door swung, and let the draught in.
cliffhanger: The woman at the trimmings stall has watched her all morning and not said a word.

title: The Zip
segment_text:
## Chapter 5 — The Zip

The jacket came in on Saturday over the arm of a woman of sixty-three, who put it down on the table like a cat she was proud of.

"Nineteen ninety-four," she said. "I've had it longer than I had my husband and I've been fonder of it."

Black leather gone soft as a glove, and a smell in it Alison knew — leather and petrol and the inside of somebody's garage in the eighties. The zip had gone at the bottom stop. The stop itself, pulled clean off, so the whole front parted at the hem like a curtain.

"I only need it so it fastens. I'm not fussy."

"You're a bit fussy," Alison said, "or you'd have chucked it."

The woman laughed and said, "Aye, well."

She had started again in June. Thirty-one years off it — a husband, two kids, a mortgage, a knee — and then a fella at the club had a Bonneville going for less than a decent settee, and she was out on the tops at seven on a Tuesday morning with the mist lying in the valley below her like milk in a bowl.

"Does your family not mind?"

"Our Lee thinks it's brilliant. He's been on the back." A pause. She straightened the collar of her own coat on Alison's table. "I've not told our Rachel."

"Right."

"She'd worry."

"She would."

"She'd be right to." The woman looked at her. "I'll tell her when I've had it a twelvemonth and nowt's happened, and then it's a story instead of a row."

Alison, who had not told her own son several things, said nothing at all, and got on.

She wanted a heavy-gauge zip, and there was one place in the building that had one. Which meant crossing the hall. Which meant Sonia Aktar.

She had said good morning to Sonia every day for three days and had had a nod for it, which in Ravensgate is a contract.

Aktar's Trimmings was pitch 4 and had been Aktar's Trimmings since 1979. Drawers to the ceiling, labelled in two alphabets in a hand that had got smaller as the years went on. Sonia was thirty-eight and watched everything in that hall and said about a third of it.

"Number eight, open-end, black," Alison said. "Twenty-four inch if you've got it. It's for leather."

Sonia looked at her for a second longer than the sentence needed. Then she turned and opened a drawer without reading it and laid the zip on the counter.

"Twenty-two," she said. "It'll want shortening at the top."

"I know."

"I know you know."

And she took the zip and ran it flat along the brass yard-measure screwed to her counter — worn down to a shine at thirty-six inches by seventy years of thumbs — and her own thumb came down on the shine, without her looking, the way a thumb does when it has been coming home to the same place all its life.
cliffhanger: Bernie Fazakerley does not take money off anybody in their first week.

title: Her Mother's Raincoat
segment_text:
## Chapter 6 — Her Mother's Raincoat

Sunday, so the hall was shut, and she went up to Weaver's Rise with a tin of biscuits nobody had asked for.

The flat was warden-assisted, which Sylvia pronounced like a diagnosis, and had a view to the crematorium, which Sylvia described as handy, and had done, without varying it, since 2011.

"You've brought biscuits."

"I have."

"I've biscuits."

"Well, now you've more."

They had tea. Sylvia gave her the week. Bowls on Tuesday, in which a woman called Doreen had done something with the mat that would be discussed until Christmas. The committee, from which Sylvia had been asked to step down in the spring and about which she was serene in a way that fooled nobody.

"And you," Sylvia said, "are still having a think."

"I've took a table. In the Lantern."

Her mother put her cup down.

"By the north door," Alison said. "Seventy-two pound a week."

"Crabtree's old spot."

"That's it."

Sylvia looked out at the crematorium. "Well," she said. "You'll want a fan heater."

The raincoat was on the hook in the hall where it had been every Sunday of Alison's adult life. Beige, 1988, from a shop on Corn Street that no longer exists. Sylvia had bought it the year Alison did her City and Guilds. Thirty-eight years of Ravensgate rain had taken it to the weight of paper. When you lifted it off the hook it did not swing. It went with you, all of it at once, like something asleep.

Alison turned the cuff over. It had gone through, both sides, at the fold where a wrist bends.

"I'll get you a new one," she said. "There's a place in Halifax does a good one, proper cotton, and you can have it for your birthday and there's an end of it."

"No," said Sylvia.

"Mother —"

"No." Not loud. Not sharp. She said it the way you put your hand flat on a door somebody is trying to open. After a second Alison stopped pushing, because she had been pushing at that door for fifty-two years and it had never once moved.

"Let me have it, then, and I'll do the cuffs."

"You can do the cuffs."

She brought it home on the bus on her knee. She had the thread out on the table by nine, and the good needle, and the bit of matching she had been carrying in her box since about 2004 for exactly this.

She did not do it.

She sat with a cup of tea going cold and did not do it, and then she put the coat over the back of the kitchen chair to be getting on with tomorrow.

It stopped there all evening. From the doorway, in the half-light off the street, it was the shape of a woman sat with her back to you, her shoulders exactly so, and the room going quiet around her.
cliffhanger: Her mother would like to know what she is now, and will keep asking until she is told.

title: Someone Else's Chalk
segment_text:
## Chapter 7 — Someone Else's Chalk

The dress came in on the Tuesday with a woman who wanted it taking in at the waist and had a wedding in Skipton on the third.

Navy, lined, good enough cloth. Alison turned the collar to look for a label out of habit, and there it was, cream with a gold edge and the copperplate E. Ellerby's of Ravensgate. Est. 1904.

"Bought it there," the woman said. "Six year back, seven. Had it altered there and all. I'd have took it back but —" and she made a small movement of the hand that took in the whole of Corn Street.

"Let's see it on."

She saw it on, and pinned it, and wrote the ticket, and the woman went off to Bernie's for a pie.

Then she turned it inside out.

The seam had been let out at some point, by somebody who knew what they were about — old stitch line pressed flat, new one running true, allowance opened and laid down. And there on the wrong side, an inch below the waist, was a chalk mark. Two strokes and a small firm tick, the tick going away to the left and up, put there by a left hand.

Alison sat down.

She knew that hand at fifty paces. Nineteen years of it: on tickets, on the pad by the kettle, on the back of a fag packet in 2010 when the two of them had worked out between them whether Pauline could afford a caravan. Two strokes and a tick that went the wrong way, because everything Pauline did went the wrong way and came out right.

2019. She could nearly do the year off the cloth. She could nearly do the month.

They had sat three feet apart, Pauline on the window side. Pauline had known in January. She had sat on the staff consultation panel and been given a form of words, and had gone on saying good morning, and how's your Joe, and I'll put the kettle on, from January to the fourteenth of April, when the rest of them found out with the local paper. It was not a lie. Alison had been over it enough times to be sure of that. It was a silence, and a silence is worse. You cannot hold it up and say look what she's done. There is nothing in your hands.

She had not rung. Pauline had not rung. That was the twenty-first week of it.

She did the work. She unpicked the old seam and took it in the inch and a quarter it wanted and pressed it, and the whole afternoon her fingers went over that chalk line and either side of it, and she did not rub it out. It would have taken a thumb.

At half three she pressed the new seam and turned the dress the right way out, and the chalk went where the allowance went — folded in, flat to the inside of a seam that nobody would now ever open again.
cliffhanger: She has not spoken to Pauline Craddock since the fourteenth of April, and Pauline has not rung either.

title: Bernie's Pocket
segment_text:
## Chapter 8 — Bernie's Pocket

Bernie Fazakerley came down the hall on Thursday morning with her tabard over her arm and the biro behind her ear, saying, before she had arrived, "Now then. You'll not do owt with this."

The right pocket had come off. Not torn — come off, the whole of it, leaving its own shape behind in a paler blue, because forty years of a hand going in and out of a pocket is forty years of a hand going in and out of a pocket, and cloth is only cloth.

"I've had this tabard since our Denise were at school," Bernie said. "She's forty-one."

"It's had a life."

"It's had a better one than me."

Alison put her hand flat inside and felt the cloth where the pocket had been, and it was thin as a page. Bernie gave her, unasked, the history of the hall: who had been on pitch 11 before her, which was a fishmonger, and what became of him, which was Blackpool.

"I'll want to double it," Alison said. "Put a facing in behind, or it'll go again in a fortnight."

"Do what you like, love. What's the damage?"

"Six pound."

Bernie made a noise like a kettle taken off early and went up the hall, and came back four minutes later with a steak pie on a paper bag and set it down on the ticket.

"Bernie —"

"You've been here a week."

"It's not a week, it's —"

"You've been here a week," said Bernie, in the voice of a woman putting a lid on, "and I don't take money off anybody in their first week. Ask any of them. Ask Yusuf. Ask Kelly. It's not a rule I've made up this morning to be nice to you, it's forty year old, and I'll thank you not to be the first."

So Alison ate a steak pie standing up at eleven in the morning, with the paper bag round the bottom of it and her thumb through the crust, and somebody had made it and handed it to her, and it was the first time since April that anybody had put hot food into her hands. She did not say that. Bernie was three feet away, on to a man from the council.

The biro stayed behind her ear. When she wanted to write down what she owed the flour man she took a different one out of her apron.

Alison rebuilt the pocket after dinner. She cut a facing from a bit of blue drill out of her own box and set it in behind, and squared the pocket up and bar-tacked both corners the way you do a work pocket. And then, because the tabard was on her table and Bernie was fifty feet away with her back to her, she made it an inch deeper than it had been.

She never said. Bernie never noticed. All that afternoon her hand went in and out of it, down to the knuckle, as though it had always been that deep, and had always fit.
cliffhanger: Somebody has left a wedding dress on her table with no name attached to it.

title: The Second Wearer
segment_text:
## Chapter 9 — The Second Wearer

The dress was on the table when she opened up on Saturday, in a zipped carrier with no name on it, and nobody in the hall knew a thing about it — which in that hall meant somebody knew everything about it and had been asked not to say.

Alison unzipped it two inches and left it.

The young woman came at twenty past ten. Thirty-four, and she stood at the end of the table with her keys still in her hand.

"That's mine. Sorry. Hilary let me leave it. I wasn't sure I'd come."

"Well, you have."

Ivory duchesse satin, a wedding dress, 1985, made by somebody in a room with a wireless on. Long sleeves, a covered button placket to the waist, a bit of yellow at the neck where a neck had been.

"It's my mum's."

"It's lovely."

"She's fine. She's not — sorry. Everybody thinks. She's in Brighouse, she's fine, she got it down out the loft in March and said have it if you want it." The girl was talking very fast. "And I put it on. And it doesn't. I got the sleeves on. I couldn't do the back. And I've said to Craig, we'll just buy one, it's daft, and he says get it altered, and I says you can't just —"

"Take your coat off," Alison said, "and let's have a look at it inside out."

She turned the dress and laid it flat on the deal, wrong side up, and opened the back seams with her thumbs, and looked.

"Right," she said, in the voice she used for a job. "Whoever made this left an inch and a quarter down both back seams and another inch at the side. That's two and a half inch, and it's never been touched. And there's a full inch in the sleeve head, which nobody does now."

"So it'd —"

"There's plenty here," Alison said. "There's plenty here. They left plenty. It's a job of about four hours."

And the girl's shoulders came down. Not a bit of the way. Two inches, all at once, the way a curtain drops when you take the rod out — and she stood in the draught of the north door and let go of a breath she had been holding somewhere up near her ears since March.

Nobody said anything about her body. Not one word. There was a dress with an inch and a quarter in the back seams and a woman who wanted to wear it, and those are two facts about cloth.

"Come Tuesday," Alison said. "Bring your shoes."

When she had gone, Alison lifted the dress by the shoulders and held it up to the glass in the north door, and read the old allowance through the satin — a shadow, a darker band, a hand's width of cloth folded in and left there forty-one years ago by a woman at a machine who had never met this girl, and who had left her room anyway.
cliffhanger: In the morning there is a woman waiting at the north door in a suit she bought in 2009.

title: The Suit
segment_text:
## Chapter 10 — The Suit

She was at the north door before Alison had the cover off the machine, in the suit, holding her handbag in front of her with both hands.

"I'm ever so sorry. I'm early. Sorry. Are you even open? Sorry. I'll come back — sorry."

"That's four," Alison said. "Come in out of the draught."

Forty-nine. The suit was black, bought in 2009, worn twice: a funeral, and a do at a hotel where her husband's firm gave him a glass thing with his name spelled wrong on it. Thursday she had an interview. Office manager, a haulage firm, twenty-eight hours.

"It'll not fit right," she said. "I'm not the same as I was in 2009, am I. Nobody is."

"Nobody is," Alison agreed, and got her tape. "Stand normal. Don't stand nice for me. Stand how you stand."

The woman stood how she stood, which took her a moment to find.

"Eleven year I've been out," she said, to the room. "I did my mum, at the end. Four year of that. Before that it were the kids. And they give you a form, and the box says employment history. Eleven year of my life and there's nowt goes in the box."

Alison had four pins in her mouth, which was fortunate, because what she wanted to say was that she had spent twenty-six years being extremely good at a thing the world had decided was not a profession, and that there was no box on any form for that either.

"Sorry," the woman said. "You don't want all this."

"That's five," said Alison.

The trouble was the shoulder. It was a 2009 shoulder, sitting a good inch out past where the woman actually was, so that the whole suit hung off her like a coat off a chair back.

"Can you not just let it out somewhere?"

"There's nowt wrong wants letting out. It's sat out here" — she put two fingers on the seam — "and it wants to sit here. I'll take the shoulder in and lift the sleeve head half an inch. That's the whole job."

"That's all?"

"That's all there is."

She did it that morning and had her back at two. There was no mirror at the table, so she walked her down the hall to Sonia's, where there is a long one screwed to the drawers, and Sonia moved a box of bias binding off the floor in front of it without being asked.

The woman looked at herself.

And she came up. Nobody told her to. Her chin came up and her shoulders went back, and she stood on a Monday morning and looked at somebody she appeared to recognise.

She said nothing. Alison said nothing. Sonia, four feet away, said nothing at all, which for Sonia was a considerable amount of saying.

"Right," the woman said, at last.

"Right," said Alison.
cliffhanger: Somebody is coming with curtains, and she has already said she does not do curtains.
